theater: 巴士拉以南鹽沼與底格里斯下游

battle.name: 張格爾之亂
battle.theater: 巴士拉以南鹽沼與底格里斯下游
battle.brief: 張格爾之亂即阿拉伯史料所稱的津芝叛亂，戰爭列表把它編在一八二〇至一八二七年一格，史實上的起事則發生於八六九至八八三年，戰場在巴士拉以南的鹽沼與運河地帶。叛軍以沼澤游擊、水網舟隊與夜襲拖住阿拔斯軍隊十四年，最後在穆赫塔拉被長期圍城攻破；卡面的燧發步槍比此役晚近千年，並未出現在戰場上。

countries: 交戰的一方是阿拔斯王朝中央政府，另一方是以巴士拉南部鹽沼奴工為主體的起義聯盟。中央方面，哈里發是穆塔米德，但自一八六一年起中央陷入薩邁拉無政府狀態，哈里發接連更替，總督各自為政，首都財政崩潰，欠餉引發兵變，真正主持南部戰役的是哈里發之弟穆瓦法克，他在巴格達調度軍費、任命主將，前線兵力則由巴士拉與瓦西特兩省總督就地籌措。政府軍的組成是當年伊拉克軍團的常規搭配：土庫斯系奴兵騎兵居前，伊拉克步兵以弓手與長槍手為主，攻城時另調工程隊、撞槌與投石機，並有阿拉伯部族騎兵隨軍作戰；軍費靠國庫撥款與薩瓦德鹽沼農業區的地稅，而那片被開墾的沼澤正是雙方爭奪的所在。起義方沒有單一血統：核心是被販入伊拉克的東非黑奴及其受釋者，外圍有巴士拉城內的工匠、依附豪門的半自由民、小農與周邊貝都因部落。首領阿里·本·穆罕默德自稱先知與阿里後裔，在沼澤中的穆赫塔拉建都，自行徵稅、鑄幣，並在運河上組織舟隊，把一場奴工暴動變成有行政、有財政的地方政權。
countriesEn: One side was the central government of the Abbasid Caliphate; the other was a rebel coalition drawn mainly from the enslaved labour force of the salt marshes south of Basra. On the government side the caliph was al-Mu'tamid, but from 861 the centre had been paralysed by the Anarchy at Samarra: caliphs succeeded one another in quick succession, governors ruled their own districts almost unsupervised, the capital's finances collapsed, and unpaid troops mutinied. The man who actually directed the southern war was the caliph's brother al-Muwaffaq, who ran the campaign from Baghdad, raised money and appointed commanders, while the troops in the field were levied locally by the governors of Basra and Wasit. The government army was the standard Iraqi mix of the era: Turkish slave cavalry in front, Iraqi infantry whose main weapons were the bow and the spear, and, for sieges, engineers, battering rams and traction trebuchets, with Arab tribal cavalry riding along. The war was paid for from the treasury and from the land tax of the Sawad salt-marsh plantations, and those reclaimed marshes were precisely the ground both sides were fighting over. The rebel side had no single ethnic identity. Its core was the Zanj, enslaved and freed East Africans carried in through the Indian Ocean trade, ringed by craftsmen in Basra, half-freed dependants of great families, tenant peasants and a few Bedouin groups living around the city. The commander Ali ibn Muhammad proclaimed himself a prophet and a descendant of Ali, made his capital at al-Mukhtarah in the marshes south of Basra, levied taxes, struck his own coin and organised a boat force on the canals, turning what had begun as a slave rising into a regional power with its own administration and finances.
people: Ali ibn Muhammad is the only figure in this rising whose name survives in the sources. The chronicles describe him as born near Rayy in Persia, his paternal line belonging to the tribe of Abd al-Qays, and he spent part of his youth in Samarra among the powerful dependants of Caliph al-Muntasir. In 863 he went to Bahrayn in eastern Arabia, posed as a Shiite and raised support, and after that rising collapsed he moved to Basra, where he tried to exploit the fighting between the city's Bilaliyyah and Sa'diyyah factions. Having failed he was seized by the provincial authorities and sent to Wasit, escaped, and spent a year in Baghdad, where he claimed descent from the grandson of Zayd ibn Ali and called himself a Zaydi. When factional strife broke out in Basra again in 869 he returned, began moving among the black slaves working the marshes, promised them freedom and a share of wealth, and gradually built a following, calling himself the Chief of the Zanj. He kept up the pretension of Alid descent while borrowing the egalitarian doctrine of the Kharijites, that the most qualified man ought to rule even if he is a slave. Caliph al-Mu'tamid, himself constrained by unpaid soldiers, could not be relied on. The real commander was the regent al-Muwaffaq, who sent his son Abu al-'Abbas with the main force in 879 and joined the offensive in person the following year, combining sweeps through the countryside with offers of generous terms to those who surrendered. The names of the caliphal commanders appear in the chronicles in conflicting transliterations; the general credited with the final siege and the pursuit is Muhammad ibn Isa al-Juludi, while appointments and finance were handled in Baghdad by the vizierate.

kits: The card shows a flintlock musket, and that weapon has no battlefield presence in this war. The Zanj revolt at issue began in 869 and ended in 883; the flintlock was a mature European mechanism of the seventeenth century, nearly a millennium later, and the earliest hand-held gunpowder weapons in the Islamic world do not appear until the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The musket therefore cannot be written into the order of battle; on this card it stands for the later end of the firearm line. The insurgents actually fought with ninth-century equipment: composite bows, straight Arab swords, spears and javelins, wooden-framed hides covered round shields, iron or bronze helmets, lamellar armour of leather thongs and riveted plates, and a great many horses, since the raiding parties moved on horseback and by boat through the water country. Their camps were built of reeds and mud plaster and burned readily, so an assault almost always ended in fire. Weapons came from captures, from raids on government posts and from their own smiths, and the rebels kept metalworkers and arrow-makers busy. The caliphal army was the usual combination of heavy cavalry and infantry, with scaling ladders, rams and stone-throwing engines for the sieges; the Arabic sources record both sides using naphtha projectors and fire-pots, and fire was especially important against the reed-built strongholds in the marshes. The claim that the rebels had war elephants does occur in the sources, but is generally treated by later scholars as a legend rather than a deployment.

tactics: In its first phase the rising was kept alive by very small detachments dispersed along the edge of the marshes. They struck government patrols, relay stations and small camps at night, took weapons, horses, food and prisoners, freed their own people, and burned what they could not carry away so as to delay the counter-attack. Once established they raised fortresses in the marsh, formed a flotilla of flat-bottomed boats to work the canals, avoided meeting regular cavalry in the open, and in the areas they held they levied taxes and struck coin, turning raiding into a local government with its own revenue. The government's early defeats were not caused by inferior equipment but by poor intelligence and supply: once an expeditionary column left the main tracks and pushed into the marsh, its detachments and posts lost contact with one another and were destroyed piecemeal. Between 870 and 876 the two sides traded the ground repeatedly across the Sawad and al-Ahwaz, the rebels taking towns and widening their tax base while the government fell back on the fortified towns and rebuilt its lines of supply. From 879 the government took the initiative, massed troops to clear Iraq and al-Ahwaz and drove the rebels back towards their capital al-Mukhtarah. A long siege opened in February 881, run together with generous offers of pardon that broke the personal ties holding the rebel side together. The town fell in August, the survivors were hunted through the marshes, and the leader was betrayed by one of his own.

data: The chronology is the firmest part of this war. The rising opened in September 869, al-Mukhtarah fell in August 883, giving about fourteen years; the siege itself ran from February 881, roughly two and a half years; and on 30 November 883 Abu al-'Abbas entered Baghdad and held a victory parade. Geographically the rebels reached their furthest extent in the marshes between Basra and Wasit and then pushed north-west along the Tigris, at one point coming to within about fifty miles, some eighty kilometres, of Baghdad; the fighting core lay in the salt marshes and canal network south of Basra. On numbers of troops, the government committed several large armies in turn and the figures given in different books disagree, so the safe statement is that these were among the best equipped forces of the year. On losses, modern work places the dead in the tens of thousands, while the figure of five hundred thousand given by the ninth-century historian al-Mas'udi is regarded as gross exaggeration; the leader was captured and, according to the accounts, a number of chiefs were killed with him, while the number who surrendered without a fight cannot be counted with certainty and was plainly large. Rebel seizures and collected revenue survive only as general statements, with no figures that can be checked.

cause: The rising had two roots. The first was the working of the Sawad salt-marsh plantations, which needed a large labour force; East African slaves were herded into work camps in the marshes to dig canals and clear silt, treated badly, and there had already been two earlier risings in 689-90 and 694, both small and quickly crushed. The second was that the Abbasid centre had fallen into the Anarchy at Samarra after 861: caliphs changing rapidly, unpaid troops mutinying more than once, the treasury close to bankruptcy, tax revenue leaking away, governors left almost entirely to their own devices in their provinces, and the centre in no position to send troops south. The factional fighting inside Basra gave Ali ibn Muhammad his opening; after his failed rising in Bahrayn he turned to the marshes and promised the black slaves freedom and wealth, turning a population labouring for years in the salt flats into an army with a common cause. At the same time the advance of Ya'qub ibn al-Layth of the Saffarids into al-Ahwaz drew off troops the government might otherwise have sent, leaving the southern theatre even thinner.

impact: The most direct consequences fell on the system of slavery. The Zanj revolt came to be treated by later writers as the end of the large-scale import of East African slaves into Iraq: the southern marshes still needed labour, but the form of service changed, and from the tenth century black slaves were no longer used in bulk on the land but increasingly in household work, a shift that altered the labour structure of late Abbasid society. Politically the centre spent heavily in men and money and was delayed in its response to the Saffarids and to Byzantium; al-Muwaffaq still held real power after the war, and his son Abu al-'Abbas took the caliphate as al-Mu'tadid in 883. In the register of ideas, this movement, which carried religious reform and the emancipation of slaves in one, is ranked by later Arabic historians among the fiercest disturbances of the late Abbasid period, and it stands as one of the rare large-scale workings of the egalitarian claim that the most qualified man ought to rule in the early Islamic world. Militarily it left a standard lesson: regular cavalry loses cohesion when a roadless marsh and its canals are given to the raiders. For the historical record, the detail with which ninth-century Arabic chronicles and geographical works describe these fourteen years is hardly matched in early Islamic sources, and they remain a principal source for the institutions of the southern salt marshes and for provincial military life.

result: In August 883, after the long siege and the offers of pardon, al-Mukhtarah fell. The sources differ on whether Ali ibn Muhammad was killed in the fighting or taken alive, and the better supported account is that he was betrayed by one of his own and captured; his head was then impaled on a lance, set on a boat and carried up and down the canals for all to see. The rest either surrendered or scattered, the war ended in victory for the caliphal army, and the centre regained the Sawad salt-marsh plantations and the waterways south of Basra. On 30 November 883 Abu al-'Abbas entered Baghdad and held a victory parade in which the head was shown again, as a demonstration to the capital. According to the accounts the leader was taken to Baghdad and executed, with a number of chiefs, said to be several dozen, killed at the same time; large numbers of slaves were drawn back into government troops and estates, and the labour arrangements of the southern salt marshes were reorganised. For this card the point is one of chronology: the outcome of the war belongs to the ninth century, nearly a millennium before the flintlock musket, since gunpowder firearms reached the Islamic world only in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries and the seventeenth-century flintlock came far later still, so the two have no shared battlefield at all.
